US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said that the administration was examining whether a ban on diesel exports was feasibile, after US President Donald Trump said he backed such a ban amid a record surge in diesel prices, Reuters reported.

Their remarks came as Republican candidates in some of the tightest election races in November called for the measure as a way to curb record fuel prices.

Diesel prices have shot to record highs in the US and Europe as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel ... I've called for it. I've called for it within my people," Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, according to Reuters.

Speaking at the same meeting, Bessent said, "We are examining whether a full or partial ban would work".

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Colombia withdraws its ICJ intervention in Gaza genocide case
item.description:
Colombia withdraws its ICJ intervention in Gaza genocide case

Colombia has withdrawn its Article 63 declaration of intervention in South Africa’s Gaza genocide case against Israel, according to the International Court of Justice.

In a statement, the ICJ said Colombia informed the court about its decision on 18 September. 

According to the ICJ, Article 63 gives states that are not parties to a dispute the right to intervene when the case concerns the construction of a convention to which they are also parties.

It added that the court's interpretation of the relevant parts of that convention in its decision will then be equally binding on those states.

Colombia's move does not affect the proceedings in the case, which South Africa brought against Israel in December 2023.

Under President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on August 7, Colombia has reversed several policies adopted during the previous government led by Gustavo Petro, which included severing ties with Israel, calling it a genocidal government and halting coal exports.

The surge followed disruption to the kingdom's East-West pipeline, which normally allows Saudi crude to bypass the Strait of Hormuz altogether by moving oil overland to the Red Sea coast. 

Kpler's analysts say some of the six vessels involved in the loading surge had already been flagged for dark ship-to-ship transfers or unusual port calls in the previous six weeks, suggesting the rerouting seen on 21 September “sits on top of a longer-running pattern of changing vessel behaviour”.

Ras Tanura just recorded its busiest loading day since before the war.

Israeli restrictions have stalled the delivery of more than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities to help injured children in Gaza, according to ABC News.

Two shipments from New South Wales-based charity Kids on Wheels Alliance arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while a third, from Wheelchairs for Kids based in Western Australia, arrived in October 2025. 

Both remain stuck in storage facilities managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization (JHCO).

At one of those sites on the outskirts of the Jordanian capital Amman, Abdullah Al-Balawi, a doctor with the Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA), told the ABC:

"These wheelchairs that are dedicated to Gaza's amputee children and those paralysed as a result of the war … they do not pose any threat," he said.

The JHCO said the Israeli agency responsible for aid coordination in Gaza, COGAT, had blocked the chairs from getting into Gaza, but an Israeli government source denied that an application for the Australian wheelchairs had been rejected.

COGAT did not answer the ABC's specific questions about the Australian donations, but in a general response said it had let thousands of wheelchairs into the strip during the war, ABC reported.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, and main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, dipped to $98.91 and $89.93 per barrel respectively in early Asian trade -- well below the symbolic $100 mark they have smashed repeatedly since the Middle Eat war broke out in February.

The three-hour meeting was "very good", "very productive" and "they have another one scheduled in the very near future", Trump told reporters as he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump's announcement came just hours after he delivered a bellicose address to the UN in which he said he faced a "big decision" on whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".

Report by AFP

item.description:
Report: Hormuz traffic on Tuesday below 10-day average

Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.

The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage.
All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT.

One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data.

The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Iran conflict.
Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, another maritime chokepoint on the southwest tip of Yemen and a vital trade route for oil between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

The data showed 14 vessels heading towards the Red Sea and 8 towards the Gulf of Aden. 
The number compared with an average of around 26 ships using the strait in the past 10 days.

Report by Reuters

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] No peace with Israel 'if rights of Syrians are usurped', Sharaa says
item.description:
No peace with Israel 'if rights of Syrians are usurped', Sharaa says

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 00:01
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the Syrian president said areas occupied by Israel since 2024, as well as the Golan Heights, remain core concerns
Former US diplomat Brett McGurk, left, speaks to Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa at an event hosted by the Atlantic Council in New York City on 22 September 2026 (Screengrab/YouTube)
Off

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said on Tuesday that despite ongoing discussions with Israel, he could not entertain the notion of diplomatic relations while Israel carries out air strikes on his country and occupies his birthplace of the Golan Heights. 

"Since the fall of the former regime, Israel is repeating its attacks and aggressions against Syria," Sharaa said at an event hosted by the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.

"It [Israel] is occupying new territories. There are territories that have been occupied after the 8th of December 2024," he said, speaking through a translator and referring to the day he led Syrian rebel factions into the capital, and former president Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia.

"Until today, it is doing incursions, arrests inside Syria, and bombing different locations in Syria. Syria still chose to go through diplomacy and to solve that problem through talk and negotiations, as well as seeking the help of countries that are friendly to Israel, including the United States," he added.

"However, things are not easy." 

The Israelis, Sharaa said, will often "reach 90 percent" of a security agreement with Syria before suddenly withdrawing "for different reasons". 

"We need to protect the security and the rights of the Syrians before we can talk about peace," he maintained. "We cannot talk about peace if the rights of Syrians are usurped."

US President Donald Trump - who has made no secret of admiring Sharaa - decided during his first term in office in 2018 to unilaterally recognise the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights as part of Israel. The move had long been on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's wishlist.

'We cannot talk about peace if the rights of Syrians are usurped'

- Ahmed al-Sharaa, Syrian President

The United Nations recognises the Golan as occupied Syrian territory. 

"There is no discussion about those territories and to whom they belong," Sharaa said, adding that when he visited Trump at the White House last year, he suggested the president give away a US state instead of territory he doesn't own. 

"I made a joke with him when he said the Golan Heights [is within] the sovereignty of Israel. I said why don't you give New Jersey to the Israelis? You don't own Golan Heights to give it to them, but you own New Jersey, and I believe that New Jersey is full of Democrats, and they are not voting for Trump. So it will be good to give it to the Israelis."

The story elicited laughter among the crowd.

"Maybe we need an international committee to discuss those concerns in order to verify what is only a perception [and] what is genuine concern" about the Golan Heights, Sharaa said.

"We don't want to always be under the umbrella or under the perception that we are talking about the concerns of Israel."

Syria can 'empower the Lebanese government'

Trump has in the past floated the idea of having Syrian forces help demilitarise Hezbollah in Lebanon, toward a Lebanon-Israel peace deal.

The matter appeared entirely a non-starter, given the fragile state of post-war Syria, and Beirut's tense relationship with Damascus given Hezbollah has long backed Assad's grip on power - oftentimes violently. 

Hezbollah remains one of the most powerful military entities in the region.

Asked about his role in "stabilising" his neighbour, which has come under fierce Israeli attacks since Hezbollah launched rockets in support of its ally Hamas in October 2023, Sharaa said Syria can "empower the Lebanese government to have better institutions". 

"Not to have any weapons working or functioning outside the rule of law or the the Lebanese state as well, [and] at the same time also to improve the Lebanese society and economic conditions there, in order to overcome the problems that the Syrian regime caused in Lebanon," he added.

"So we are engaging a best mechanism for political reform."

Tuesday's discussion with Sharaa was led by Brett McGurk, who worked with four presidents from both parties on Middle East issues, and maintains a hawkish pro-Israel and pro-US interventionist position.

He last worked in the White House under Joe Biden, where the return of the Israeli captives in Gaza became his paramount file.

The Israeli paper Haaretz recently revealed that Hamas offered to release all the captives within 24 hours of the 7 October 2023 attacks, but that the US and Israel turned down the offer. Biden's top diplomat at the time, Antony Blinken, called the reporting false. 

McGurk's first question to Sharaa was about the 11 September 2001 attacks, given they were both sitting in New York City, and it had recently been the 25th anniversary. 

"In 2013, you pledged allegiance to Ayman al-Zawahiri, who was the leader of al-Qaeda at the time, and of course was a mastermind to that attack... I just want to give you the opportunity... to renounce that former pledge."

Sharaa responded: "9/11, I had nothing to do with that at the time. I was 13 years old."

McGurk pushed again on the renunication.

"There are so many questions that are part of the past now, so maybe we need to update ourselves," Sharaa replied. "I don't believe that it is appropriate time to discuss things that happened 25 years ago. I was at a different age, and the conditions in the region were different, and they were pushing a lot of young people to go into that direction because of the pressure in that region."

Less than two years ago, Sharaa had a $10m bounty on his head, thanks to a US State Department terrorist designation that listed him alongside the top leaders of Isis in Syria.

He was known by his nom-de-guerre then, Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, and he led the al-Qaeda offshoot Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham all the way to the presidential palace in December 2024.

As a young man he'd spent six years in a US prison in Iraq for joining militias to fight the Americans after the 2003 invasion. 

Now, however, he has become "part of this action" of ousting the Assad family, he told McGurk.

"Lifting that injustice is a noble act that any person will be honoured to do."

Governance

After two US army soldiers and a civilian interpreter were killed last year following an ISIS attack on a joint American-Syrian convoy in central Syria, Sharaa said his government is still going through "several levels" of building out a new security infrastructure for the country.

Trying to dismantle militias and bring all weaponry under control of the state, as well as vetting and recruiting for a national army all at once can cause "incidents", Sharaa said. 

"There were several similar incidents, but they were not with American soldiers," he noted.

McGurk asked if Sharaa would be open to US troops returning in large numbers to Syria to train the new national army. 

"There was a prior decision to withdraw troops from Iraq, and the Americans were upset because of that. And you were one of the people who were upset because of that decision," the Syrian president responded.

How Turkey helped engineer Ahmed al-Sharaa's rise to power
Read More »

"But I believe things happened very well and very smoothly," he noted of Trump's withdrawal of US troops from Syria. "There, the withdrawal was very safe, and the region remained calm. No problems happened because of that vacuum, and the Syrian state and Syrian forces took control over the area, and [Kurdish forces] in the northeast were integrated [into Syria's military]."

"Emptying Syria from foreign bases... that is a good approach," he added.

That includes Russia, he confirmed, which had 170 bases across the country that have now been narrowed down to just two - and both of those bases will be used for training the Syrian military, Sharaa said. 

On how he plans to tackle decentralisation given the many distinct ethnic and religious groups in Syria, Sharaa deferred to what he described as "old law" that his government can build on, as it devises the path that will elect a new president three years from now. 

"There are wide powers for the governorates in the election of the municipal councils," he said. 

"The People's Assembly is going to appoint a committee that is going to review the different laws in Syria, and another committee that will start drafting the constitution. And I believe that will be completed before the end of the five years [transition period]."

When asked, Sharaa did not rule out a run for election himself.

Sharaa is expected to give an address at the United Nations General Assembly later this week and last year he became the first Syrian leader in 60 years to stand at the famed podium.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] PM’s new anti-disinformation unit won’t target ‘domestic political dissent’, defence secretary says – UK politics live
item.description:
Wes Streeting told GB News: ‘We’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent’

Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what felt like the middle of the night in UK time and he announced that he is setting up what he is calling a National Centre for Information Defence.

Burnham said this was necessary because “over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality”.

In recent years we have seen an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies.

Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears.

One of the great things about Britain, and one of the things that I have a responsibility to defend, is the freedom and democracy that we all enjoy.

And that includes the freedom to disagree, the freedom for people to challenge their government, to challenge government policy, to criticise robustly what we are doing and then to have the opportunity to choose a different government.

We’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent.
